title: OS Basics & Processes
summary: What an operating system is for, how programs cross into the kernel, what a process really is, how processes are created, switched and reaped, and how they talk to each other.

lessons.title: What an operating system does
lessons.summary: The three jobs of an OS (abstraction, resource management, protection), the line between kernel and user space, and how monolithic, micro- and hybrid kernels draw it differently.
lessons.body:
Run `cat notes.txt` and a dozen things happen that `cat` never asks for. Something finds the file on a disk it has never heard of, loads the program into memory that another program might also want, gives it a slice of a CPU shared with hundreds of other processes, and stops it from reading your browser's memory. That something is the **operating system**.

An OS is the software layer between hardware and programs. It does three jobs, and almost every OS feature is one of them.

## Job 1: abstraction

Hardware is ugly. A disk is an array of numbered blocks with a vendor-specific command set. A network card is a ring of DMA buffers. A CPU is a set of registers and a program counter.

The OS turns these into clean, portable ideas:

| Hardware | Abstraction |
|---|---|
| CPU cores | Processes and threads |
| Physical RAM | Virtual address spaces |
| Disk blocks | Files and directories |
| NIC, packets | Sockets |
| Keyboard, screen | Terminals, file descriptors |

File descriptors give many resources a common `read`, `write` and `close` interface, though their semantics differ. Regular files are opened with `open`; pipes and sockets normally come from `pipe` and `socket`. Not every resource or operation fits this interface.

```c
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main(void) {
    char buf[4096];
    int fd = open("notes.txt", O_RDONLY);
    ssize_t n;
    while ((n = read(fd, buf, 4096)) > 0)
        write(1, buf, n); /* 1 = stdout */
    close(fd);
    return 0;
}
```

This minimal illustration omits error handling and partial-write retries; a robust copy must handle both. It has no idea whether `notes.txt` lives on ext4, on NFS across the network, or in RAM on tmpfs. The OS hides it.

## Job 2: resource management

There is one set of hardware and many programs that want it. The OS is the referee.

- **CPU time**: the scheduler decides which runnable thread gets each core and for how long.
- **Memory**: the virtual memory system decides which pages live in RAM and which are evicted to disk or dropped.
- **I/O bandwidth**: the block layer queues and orders disk requests.
- **Everything else**: file descriptors, PIDs, network ports, GPU time.

Good resource management means **multiplexing**. In *time* (taking turns on a CPU) and in *space* (each process gets a share of RAM). The goals conflict: fairness, throughput, low latency and low power cannot all be maximised together. Much of OS design is choosing which to favour.

## Job 3: protection and isolation

If any program could write to any memory or talk to the disk controller directly, one buggy program could crash the machine, and one malicious program could read everyone's secrets.

The OS enforces boundaries:

- Each process gets its **own virtual address space**. An ordinary load in A uses A's mappings, not B's. Explicit shared mappings and authorised process-memory interfaces are exceptions.
- The kernel controls access to device registers, page tables and interrupt settings; it can delegate selected device mappings or I/O permissions to user-space drivers.
- Permissions (user IDs, file modes, capabilities) gate access to shared resources.

This needs **hardware help**. The CPU has at least two privilege levels. On x86 these are **rings**: ring 0 for the kernel, ring 3 for applications. ARM calls them exception levels (EL0 for user, EL1 for the kernel). Privileged instructions, like loading a new page table, fault if run from user mode.

> [!note] Protection is the foundation
> Abstraction and resource management are only enforceable because of protection. If a program could bypass the kernel, it could ignore the scheduler and the file permissions too.

## Kernel space and user space

The **kernel** is the part of the OS that runs in privileged mode. Everything else, including your shell, `systemd`, the desktop and your apps, runs in **user space**.

```
 +-------------------------------+
 | apps: bash, nginx, chrome     |  user
 | libraries: libc, libssl       |  space
 +---------- syscall API --------+  -------
 | kernel: scheduler, VM, VFS,   |  kernel
 | network stack, drivers        |  space
 +-------------------------------+
 | hardware: CPU, RAM, disk, NIC |
 +-------------------------------+
```

User code reaches the kernel only through a narrow, controlled door: **system calls** (next lesson). The available syscall set depends on architecture and kernel version. The C library (`glibc`, `musl`) wraps them in friendly functions like `printf` and `fopen`.

A common confusion: "the operating system" in casual use means the whole distribution (kernel, shell, utilities, desktop). In OS theory it usually means the kernel. Linux, strictly, is only a kernel; Ubuntu is an OS built on it.

## Where to draw the line: kernel designs

What belongs inside the privileged kernel? Every line of kernel code can crash the whole machine or open a security hole, so less is safer. But crossing the user/kernel boundary costs time, so more in the kernel is faster. Three answers have emerged.

### Monolithic kernels

Everything that is "OS" runs in kernel space as one big program: scheduler, memory manager, file systems, network stack, and device drivers. Components call each other with plain function calls.

- **Examples**: Linux, FreeBSD, traditional Unix.
- **Pro**: fast. A file read goes from the VFS to ext4 to the block layer to the NVMe driver without any boundary crossing.
- **Con**: a bug in any driver runs with full privilege. A bad GPU driver can corrupt file system memory and panic the kernel.

Linux softens this with **loadable kernel modules** (`modprobe`, `lsmod`), so drivers need not be compiled in. But a loaded module still runs in ring 0 with no isolation. It is a packaging trick, not a protection boundary. **eBPF** is a newer route: small programs checked by a verifier before the kernel runs them, constraining extensions according to the verifier and runtime rules; verifier or kernel bugs can still undermine that protection.

### Microkernels

Keep the kernel tiny: address spaces, threads, scheduling and **inter-process communication (IPC)**. Drivers, file systems and network stacks run as ordinary user-space **servers**.

```
  app      fs server   net server  driver
   |           |           |          |
 --+---- IPC --+---- IPC --+----------+--
 |  microkernel: threads, memory, IPC   |
 ---------------------------------------
```

- **Examples**: the L4 family (including **seL4**), QNX, MINIX 3. QNX runs in many car infotainment and industrial systems.
- **Pro**: isolation. A crashed driver is a crashed process; it can be restarted. A small kernel is easier to verify: seL4 has machine-checked functional-correctness proofs for specified configurations and assumptions, not a proof that every deployment and device is safe.
- **Con**: a file read that was one function call is now several IPC messages, each crossing into the kernel and switching address spaces. Early microkernels like Mach were notoriously slow because of this. L4 showed IPC can be made far cheaper, but the cost never reaches zero.

> [!example] The Tanenbaum–Torvalds debate
> In 1992 Andrew Tanenbaum, author of MINIX, posted that "Linux is obsolete" because it was monolithic. Linus Torvalds replied that the performance and simplicity of a monolithic design mattered more in practice. Three decades later both sides have a point: Both designs remain in use; their names alone do not establish performance, reliability or certification suitability.

### Hybrid kernels

Start from a microkernel design, then move performance-critical services back into kernel space.

- **Windows NT** (all modern Windows): a layered kernel and executive, with file systems, the network stack and most drivers running in kernel mode.
- **XNU** (macOS, iOS): the Mach microkernel combined with a large BSD layer and the IOKit driver framework, all running in kernel space.

Critics argue "hybrid" is mostly marketing: once the file system and drivers are in kernel space, the result behaves much like a monolithic kernel with a message-passing internal structure. Both macOS and Windows have since moved some drivers out to user space (Apple's DriverKit, Windows' User-Mode Driver Framework), which shows the trade-off is still live.

### Side by side

| | Monolithic | Micro | Hybrid |
|---|---|---|---|
| In kernel | Almost all | IPC, VM, sched | Most |
| Speed | Workload-dependent | IPC-sensitive | Workload-dependent |
| Fault isolation | Poor | Strong | Partial |
| Examples | Linux | seL4, QNX | NT, XNU |

## Real-world view

On a typical Linux server:

- Kernel image and module sizes depend on configuration, architecture, compression and installed drivers.
- Most "OS behaviour" you configure is policy in user space: `systemd` starts services, `udev` names devices, NetworkManager configures interfaces. The kernel provides mechanism; user space chooses policy.
- When you hit a kernel bug, you get a **kernel panic** or an **oops**, and with a monolithic kernel the safe response is often to reboot.

The **mechanism versus policy** split is worth remembering. The kernel provides "a process can be given a CPU for a time slice"; something decides *which* process and *how long*. Keeping these apart lets policy change without rewriting mechanism.

## Common misconceptions

- **"The OS is always running."** User code can run directly on the CPU until a system call, interrupt or exception transfers control. Kernel threads also execute scheduled background work; another core can be running kernel code at the same time. The OS is more like a referee who steps in when the whistle blows.
- **"User space is slower."** User instructions run at the same speed as kernel instructions. What costs time is *crossing* the boundary.
- **"Modules make Linux a microkernel."** No. Modules are loaded into the same privileged address space.

> [!note] Content gap: deployment assurances
> No benchmark, market-share survey or certified device design is supplied. Kernel categories alone do not guarantee speed or safety. seL4 guarantees depend on verified configuration and hardware assumptions, including DMA behaviour; fault isolation is not a complete safety case.

## Key takeaways
- An OS does three jobs: abstracts hardware into processes, files and sockets; manages shared resources; and protects programs from each other.
- Protection relies on hardware privilege levels (x86 rings, ARM exception levels) and per-process virtual address spaces.
- The kernel runs privileged; everything else runs in user space and enters the kernel only through system calls, interrupts and exceptions.
- Monolithic kernels (Linux) are fast but give every driver full privilege; microkernels (seL4, QNX) isolate services at the cost of IPC; hybrids (Windows NT, XNU) sit in between.
- The kernel provides mechanism; user space largely decides policy.

questions.prompt: A program uses `read(fd, buf, n)` through the same interface for a regular file, pipe or TCP socket, even though details such as blocking and short reads differ. Which job of the OS does this illustrate?

options.text: Resource management
options.explanation: Resource management is about sharing scarce hardware (CPU time, RAM) between competitors. Here nothing is being shared out; the point is the uniform interface.

options.text: Abstraction
options.explanation: Correct. The OS hides the very different hardware and kernel subsystems behind one interface: the file descriptor and `read`.

options.text: Protection
options.explanation: Protection is about stopping programs harming each other or the kernel. A uniform `read` interface does not by itself stop anything.

options.text: Scheduling
options.explanation: Scheduling decides which thread runs on a CPU. It is a part of resource management and unrelated to the interface `read` presents.

questions.workedExample:
Ask what the feature *gives the programmer*:

1. The SSD, the pipe and the socket are implemented by completely different code (a block driver, a kernel buffer, the TCP stack).
2. The program sees none of that: it sees a small integer and calls `read`.
3. Turning messy, varied hardware into one clean concept is **abstraction**.

Resource management would be the kernel deciding *how much* disk bandwidth this program gets; protection would be the kernel refusing access to a file it doesn't own.

questions.prompt: Why can an ordinary user program without delegated device mappings or I/O permission not directly control the disk controller?

options.text: Device registers are only accessible in privileged (kernel) mode, so the CPU and MMU stop user-mode code from touching them
options.explanation: The kernel normally withholds the necessary mappings and I/O permissions. Hardware enforces that policy; selected drivers can receive explicitly delegated access.

options.text: Disk controllers only accept commands from PID 1
options.explanation: PIDs are an OS-level concept the disk controller knows nothing about. The hardware enforces privilege by CPU mode, not by process ID.

options.text: The disk is encrypted, so raw access would return garbage
options.explanation: Encryption is optional and unrelated to whether the process has authorised device access.

options.text: It can, but the C library doesn't expose a function for it
options.explanation: This treats the restriction as a missing API. The block is enforced by hardware: device access is privileged, so it would fault no matter what library you used.

questions.workedExample: An ordinary process lacks device mappings and I/O permissions, so an unauthorised access faults. It normally requests file operations through a syscall. The kernel can deliberately expose selected device memory to a user-space driver, as Linux UIO does; user mode alone does not forbid every device access.

questions.prompt: Which of these runs in **kernel space** on a standard Linux system?

options.text: The `bash` shell
options.explanation: The shell is a normal user program. Its name sounds 'system-level', but it has no special privilege.

options.text: `systemd` (PID 1)
options.explanation: PID 1 is special for process management, but it is an ordinary user-space program. It uses system calls like any other process.

options.text: `glibc`, the C library
options.explanation: glibc is a user-space library linked into programs. It wraps system calls but does not run with kernel privilege.

options.text: The ext4 file system driver
options.explanation: Correct. Linux is monolithic: file systems such as ext4 run inside the kernel, in ring 0, whether built in or loaded as a module.

questions.workedExample:
Sort each candidate by whether it runs with CPU privilege:

| Component | Where |
|---|---|
| systemd | user space (PID 1) |
| glibc | user space library |
| ext4 | kernel |
| bash | user space |

In a monolithic kernel like Linux, file systems, the network stack and drivers all live in the kernel. A common trap is to assume anything 'important' such as PID 1 must be in the kernel.

questions.prompt: Suppose a fault in an in-kernel Linux network driver corrupts kernel state, while a comparable fault in an isolated QNX driver process is contained and the service can be restarted. Which design difference explains this?

options.text: QNX runs the driver in ring 0 but with a watchdog timer
options.explanation: If the driver ran in ring 0 its wild write could still corrupt the kernel. A watchdog can detect a hang, not prevent memory corruption.

options.text: QNX has better error handling in its C compiler
options.explanation: The compiler does not decide what a wild pointer write can reach. The difference is which address space and privilege level the driver runs in.

options.text: Linux runs drivers in kernel space with full privilege; QNX is a microkernel that runs drivers as isolated user-space processes
options.explanation: Correct. In a monolithic kernel a driver shares the kernel's address space, so a bad write can corrupt anything. In a microkernel the driver is a separate process, so the MMU confines the damage.

options.text: Linux loads drivers as modules, and modules are less stable than built-in code
options.explanation: Loaded and built-in code run identically in ring 0. Being a module changes packaging, not isolation.

questions.workedExample: An in-kernel driver shares privileged memory, so its corruption can affect unrelated kernel state. A driver in a separate process has a smaller accessible address space and can be supervised for restart. Actual containment also depends on shared memory, device/DMA permissions and dependencies; restart is not an automatic guarantee of uninterrupted service. IPC and scheduling add costs that depend on the implementation.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Linux **loadable kernel modules** are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: They let drivers be added to a running kernel without rebooting
options.explanation: Correct. `modprobe` or `insmod` loads a module's code into the running kernel.

options.text: A loaded module runs in kernel mode with the same privilege as the rest of the kernel
options.explanation: Correct. There is no isolation boundary between a module and core kernel code; a module bug can crash the system.

options.text: They turn Linux into a microkernel, because drivers are separate from the core
options.explanation: Wrong: separate *files* are not separate *address spaces*. A microkernel runs services as user processes; modules run in ring 0.

options.text: A crashing module is automatically restarted by the kernel, like a QNX driver
options.explanation: Wrong. A crash in a module is a kernel oops or panic, exactly like a bug in built-in code.

options.text: They reduce the size of the kernel image that must be loaded at boot
options.explanation: Correct. Drivers that aren't needed for every boot can be left out of the core image and loaded on demand.

questions.workedExample:
Separate packaging from privilege:

- **Packaging**: modules are separate `.ko` files, loaded on demand (so A and E are true).
- **Privilege**: once loaded, the code is linked into kernel memory and runs in ring 0 (B true).

Because there is no MMU boundary, nothing confines a module's bugs, which rules out C and D. Modules are a convenience for a monolithic kernel, not a step towards a microkernel.

questions.prompt: A colleague says: "The OS is always running in the background, using some CPU to supervise every program." What's the most accurate correction?

options.text: Ordinary instructions run directly in user mode; syscalls, exceptions and interrupts enter the kernel, and scheduled kernel threads can perform background work
options.explanation: The kernel does not interpret every instruction. Hardware enforces protection, while entry events and scheduled kernel work give it CPU time.

options.text: The kernel interprets each user instruction to check it is safe
options.explanation: That would be emulation and would be enormously slow. Hardware privilege checks let user code run natively and trap only on forbidden operations.

options.text: The kernel only runs at boot; after that, programs manage themselves
options.explanation: Without the kernel regaining control, one program in an infinite loop could hog the CPU forever, and nothing could handle I/O or page faults.

options.text: Right: the kernel runs on a dedicated core reserved for it
options.explanation: General-purpose kernels like Linux do not reserve a core. They run on whichever core triggered the entry.

questions.workedExample: On one core, a user thread can execute directly until a syscall, exception or interrupt enters kernel code. The scheduler may then run another user thread or a kernel thread. Different cores can execute user and kernel code concurrently. Timer-based preemption can prevent a normal time-sharing task from monopolising a core; the kernel does not supervise each instruction in software.

questions.prompt: In a microkernel, an application reads a file. The file system and the disk driver are separate user-space servers. Roughly how many address-space crossings does this need, compared with a monolithic kernel?

options.text: Zero: microkernels use shared memory so no crossings are needed
options.explanation: Shared memory can carry bulk data, but setting it up and signalling still goes through the kernel. Microkernels are defined by IPC through the kernel.

options.text: Fewer, because the microkernel is smaller
options.explanation: A smaller kernel does less itself, so more work moves to other processes and the number of crossings goes up, not down.

options.text: The same: one syscall in, one return out
options.explanation: That is the monolithic count. In a microkernel the kernel only passes messages; the real work happens in other processes, which adds crossings.

options.text: Several: app to kernel to FS server, FS server to kernel to driver, and replies back the same way
options.explanation: Correct. Each hop is an IPC through the kernel and a switch of address space. A one-syscall operation becomes a chain of messages, which is the microkernel's main performance cost.

questions.workedExample:
Trace the request:

```
Monolithic:
app -> kernel (VFS->ext4->driver)
    -> back to app
= 1 round trip

Microkernel:
app -> kernel -> FS server
FS  -> kernel -> disk driver
drv -> kernel -> FS (reply)
FS  -> kernel -> app (reply)
= 4 IPC hops, each an
  address-space switch
```

This is why L4's big contribution was making IPC very cheap: the design lives or dies on it.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the best example of the **mechanism versus policy** split in Linux?

options.text: glibc implements `printf` on top of `write`
options.explanation: That is a layering of abstractions (buffered formatted output over a syscall), not a split between a capability and the decision of how to use it.

options.text: Drivers are compiled as modules
options.explanation: That is packaging. It doesn't separate the ability to do something from the choice of when and how.

options.text: The kernel provides cgroups to cap a group's CPU and memory; systemd decides which services go in which group with which limits
options.explanation: Correct. The kernel offers the mechanism (resource limits on groups); a user-space manager decides the policy (which service gets 2 GB).

options.text: The kernel decides the IP address of every interface
options.explanation: Not the best example as written: address policy may be set by user-space tools, but the kernel also implements mechanisms such as IPv6 autoconfiguration. The cgroup/systemd option is the clearer capability-versus-policy split.

questions.workedExample:
Mechanism answers *how can it be done?* Policy answers *what should be done?*

1. cgroups: the kernel can account and cap CPU, memory and I/O for a group. That is mechanism.
2. systemd unit files say `MemoryMax=2G` for one service and not another. That is policy.
3. Because they're separate, you can change limits by editing a unit file instead of patching the kernel.

The same pattern appears in scheduling: the kernel can preempt and switch threads; priorities and nice values let user space steer *which* thread wins.

questions.prompt: Why does a small seL4 kernel make whole-kernel functional-correctness verification more tractable than a much larger Linux configuration?

options.text: seL4 is written in a safer language than C
options.explanation: seL4's kernel is written in C; the proof covers the C code (and later work the compiled binary). The language isn't the difference.

options.text: A small kernel limits the implementation and specification that must be covered; Linux configurations can include many more privileged subsystems
options.explanation: A smaller kernel can reduce proof scope. The exact guarantee still depends on verified configuration and assumptions; user-space device authority can matter to the trusted system.

options.text: Linux has no specification, while seL4 does
options.explanation: Lacking a formal spec is part of it, but even with one, proving tens of millions of lines of rapidly changing kernel code is far beyond current verification effort.

options.text: Proofs only work for kernels without interrupts
options.explanation: seL4 handles interrupts; its proof accounts for them.

questions.workedExample: seL4 publishes proofs for particular architecture/configuration combinations. A small privileged kernel makes comprehensive reasoning more tractable, while a larger implementation and changing specification increase effort. This does not prove every device deployment safe: DMA, hardware behaviour, boot assumptions and delegated authority must satisfy the documented proof assumptions.

questions.prompt: Which statements about **hybrid kernels** such as Windows NT and XNU are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: XNU combines the Mach microkernel with a BSD layer, and both run in kernel space
options.explanation: Correct. macOS's kernel puts Mach (tasks, IPC, VM) and BSD (POSIX processes, networking, VFS) together in one privileged address space.

options.text: Windows NT runs its file systems and most drivers in kernel mode
options.explanation: Correct. NTFS and the bulk of drivers run in kernel mode, which is why a bad driver can blue-screen Windows.

options.text: Hybrid kernels get full microkernel fault isolation because their design is message-based
options.explanation: Wrong. Isolation comes from separate address spaces, not from a message-passing code style. Services in kernel space can still corrupt each other.

options.text: Critics argue they behave much like monolithic kernels in practice
options.explanation: Correct. Once the performance-critical services move into kernel space, the protection properties are monolithic.

options.text: Apple and Microsoft have both added frameworks for running some drivers in user space
options.explanation: Correct. Apple's DriverKit and Microsoft's User-Mode Driver Framework move certain drivers out for isolation, showing the trade-off is still being adjusted.

questions.workedExample:
Judge each claim by asking *what runs in ring 0?*

1. XNU: Mach + BSD + IOKit all in kernel space (A true).
2. NT: executive, file systems, most drivers in kernel mode (B true).
3. If they share one address space, a bug in one can corrupt another, so microkernel isolation is not achieved (C false, D true).
4. Moving specific drivers out (DriverKit, UMDF) buys isolation back where it matters (E true).

'Hybrid' describes the *internal structure*; the *protection* model is mostly monolithic.

questions.prompt: You're designing the OS for a medical infusion pump that must pass strict safety certification, and drivers come from third parties. A teammate proposes embedded Linux for its huge driver ecosystem. What is the strongest argument for a microkernel RTOS such as QNX or seL4 instead?

options.text: Linux cannot run on embedded hardware
options.explanation: Linux runs on countless embedded devices. The issue is assurance, not capability.

options.text: Microkernels don't need device drivers
options.explanation: They still need drivers; the drivers simply run as user-space processes.

options.text: Microkernels are always faster than Linux
options.explanation: They usually aren't: IPC adds overhead. Speed is the weakest argument here.

options.text: A small trusted kernel with drivers isolated in user space limits the impact of a buggy third-party driver and shrinks the code that must be certified
options.explanation: Correct. Certification effort scales with trusted code. Isolating untrusted drivers means a fault can be contained and the driver restarted, instead of the whole device panicking.

questions.workedExample: A small trusted kernel and isolated services can reduce the scope of some assurance arguments and contain some faults. A device safety case still includes application behaviour, deadlines, recovery, hardware and driver/DMA authority. No supplied implementation, hazard analysis or certification evidence establishes whether Linux, QNX or seL4 is suitable for this particular pump, or whether IPC overhead is acceptable.

lessons.title: System calls and CPU modes
lessons.summary: User and kernel mode, the difference between traps, exceptions and interrupts, what actually happens on a Linux x86-64 syscall, what one costs, and how the vDSO avoids the cost entirely.
lessons.body:
Ordinary programs normally access protected devices through the kernel; authorised user-space drivers are an exception. Yet `cat` reads files and `curl` sends packets. The trick is that programs don't do these things; they *ask the kernel to*. The asking mechanism is the **system call**.

The challenge is to let untrusted code ask for privileged work without letting it *become* privileged. The CPU solves this with modes and a small set of fixed entry points.

## User mode and kernel mode

At any moment a CPU core runs in one of (at least) two modes:

- **User mode**: privileged instructions fault. Only pages marked user-accessible can be touched.
- **Kernel mode**: privileged operations are available, but mappings, memory protections, hardware rules and any hypervisor still constrain accesses.

The only ways from user mode into kernel mode are events the hardware routes to **addresses the kernel chose in advance**. User code can't jump into the middle of the kernel. It can only knock on doors whose locations the kernel registered at boot.

This idea is called **limited direct execution**. Run the program directly on the CPU at full speed (direct execution), but limit what it can do, and make sure the kernel regains control when needed.

## Three ways into the kernel

| Event | Cause | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Trap (syscall) | Deliberate | `syscall`, `svc` |
| Exception (fault) | Error in current instruction | Page fault, divide by 0 |
| Interrupt | External hardware | Timer tick, NIC packet |

- **Traps** are *synchronous and intentional*: the program executes a special instruction to request a service.
- In this introductory classification, **faults** are synchronous conditions caused by the current instruction. Architectural terminology also includes deliberate traps among exceptions. Some are fixable (a page fault on a lazily allocated page; the kernel maps it and re-runs the instruction). Some are fatal (a segfault becomes `SIGSEGV`).
- **Interrupts** are *asynchronous*: a device signals the CPU regardless of what's running. The **timer interrupt** is vital, because it is how the kernel takes the CPU back from a program stuck in `while (1);`.

Terminology varies between textbooks and CPU vendors (Intel calls all of these "interrupts and exceptions"), but the distinction of deliberate versus error versus external is what matters.

## Anatomy of a Linux syscall on x86-64

Here is `write(1, "hi\n", 3)` from start to finish.

```
user: write(1, "hi\n", 3)    (glibc)
  rax = 1      syscall number (write)
  rdi = 1      arg 1: fd
  rsi = buf    arg 2: pointer
  rdx = 3      arg 3: count
  syscall      -> switch to ring 0
---------------------------------------
kernel: entry_SYSCALL_64
  preserve user stack pointer
  switch to kernel stack
  save user registers
  dispatch number -> __x64_sys_write
  validate fd, copy from user buffer
  rax = 3      bytes written
  sysret/iret   -> back to ring 3
---------------------------------------
user: glibc checks rax, returns 3
```

Key details:

1. **The syscall number** goes in `rax`. On x86-64, `read` is 0, `write` is 1 and `getpid` is 39. Numbers differ by architecture; ARM64 puts the number in `x8` and uses the `svc #0` instruction.
2. **Arguments** go in `rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9`, up to six. (`r10` replaces `rcx`, which the `syscall` instruction overwrites with the return address.)
3. **The `syscall` instruction** switches to ring 0 and jumps to the address the kernel stored in a model-specific register (`MSR_LSTAR`) at boot. User code chooses *which service*, never *where to jump*.
4. **The kernel never trusts user pointers.** It copies data in and out with `copy_from_user` and `copy_to_user`, which check that the address really belongs to user space and handle faults safely.
5. **Errors** come back as a negative value in `rax`, such as `-EBADF`. glibc turns this into a return of `-1` and sets `errno`.

You can bypass the named syscall wrapper using libc's generic `syscall()` function. It still translates errors to `-1` and `errno`; this is not raw inline assembly:

```c
#include <sys/syscall.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main(void) {
    syscall(SYS_write, 1, "hi\n", 3);
    long pid = syscall(SYS_getpid);
    return pid > 0 ? 0 : 1;
}
```

> [!tip] Watch syscalls happen
> `strace -c ls` runs `ls` and prints a table of every syscall it made, how many times, and the time spent. `strace -f -e trace=openat,read cmd` shows just those calls, following child processes. It's the single most useful tool for "why is this program slow / failing?"

## Library calls versus system calls

Not every libc function is a syscall:

| Function | Syscall? |
|---|---|
| `strlen`, `memcpy` | Never |
| `printf` | Sometimes (`write` when buffer flushes) |
| `malloc` | Sometimes (`brk` or `mmap` for more memory) |
| `read`, `open` | Always (thin wrapper) |

`printf` writes into a user-space buffer. When stdout is a terminal it's **line-buffered** and flushes on each newline. When stdout is a file or pipe it's **fully buffered** (typically 4 KiB or more), so a thousand `printf` calls may become a handful of `write` syscalls. This buffering exists precisely because syscalls are expensive.

## What a syscall costs

System calls add work beyond an ordinary function call; the size of that overhead depends on the operation and machine:

- The mode switch itself and saving and restoring registers.
- Security work on entry and exit: on CPUs affected by Meltdown, **kernel page-table isolation (KPTI)** switches page tables on every entry and exit. Spectre mitigations add further barriers.
- **Indirect cost**: the kernel's code and data displace your program's lines in the L1 cache and entries in the TLB and branch predictors. Your code runs slower for a while after returning.

> [!note] Content gap: syscall latency
> No reproducible benchmark is supplied for the original nanosecond figures. Universal function-call, syscall and vDSO timing numbers are omitted; measure the chosen CPU, kernel, mitigations and workload.

> [!example] Cost adds up
> Copying a 100 MB file with 1-byte `read` and `write` calls makes 200 million syscalls. At an explicitly hypothetical 200 ns each, that's 40 seconds of pure overhead. With a 64 KiB buffer it's around 3,200 syscalls: under a millisecond. Same data, tens of thousands of times fewer calls.

How systems reduce the cost:

- **Batching**: buffer in user space (stdio), use `readv`/`writev` to move several buffers in one call, or `sendmmsg` for several UDP packets.
- **Avoid copies**: `sendfile` and `splice` move data between file descriptors inside the kernel.
- **Shared rings**: `io_uring` lets a program queue many I/O requests in memory shared with the kernel and submit them with one call, or even none if a kernel thread polls the ring.
- **Avoid the kernel entirely**: the vDSO, next.

## The vDSO: syscalls without the syscall

Some calls are made constantly but only *read* data the kernel maintains. The classic case is `clock_gettime`: logging libraries, profilers and databases call it millions of times a second.

Linux maps a small shared library called the **vDSO** (virtual dynamic shared object) into every process. It contains user-mode code for a few calls, plus a read-only page of data the kernel keeps updated (the current time base). On x86-64 it provides `clock_gettime`, `gettimeofday`, `time` and `getcpu`.

```
$ cat /proc/self/maps | grep vdso
7ffd8a5f2000-7ffd8a5f4000 r-xp ... [vdso]
```

When glibc's `clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &ts)` runs, it calls the vDSO function, which reads the kernel's data page and the CPU's timestamp counter in user mode. No mode switch, so it avoids kernel-entry overhead when that clock and clocksource support the fast path.

> [!warning] When the vDSO falls back
> If the system clock source can't be read from user mode (for example some virtual machines using a clock source the vDSO doesn't support), the vDSO quietly falls back to a real syscall. A service that suddenly spends a lot of time in `clock_gettime` after moving to new VMs is a known symptom. Check `/sys/devices/system/clocksource/clocksource0/current_clocksource`.

## Pitfalls

- **Assuming `errno` is always valid.** It's only meaningful when the call reported failure; successful calls may leave junk in it.
- **Ignoring `EINTR`.** A blocking syscall interrupted by a signal handler may return `-1` with `errno == EINTR`. Robust code retries (or uses `SA_RESTART`).
- **Short reads and writes.** `read` can return fewer bytes than asked, for example near EOF or when fewer bytes are currently available on a pipe or socket. Loop until you have what you need.
- **Counting syscalls in hot loops.** A per-request `stat()` or `gettimeofday` (on a system without vDSO support) can dominate a fast server's profile.

## Key takeaways
- The CPU enforces user and kernel modes; user code enters the kernel only at entry points the kernel registered in advance.
- In the simplified terminology here, syscall traps are deliberate, faults are synchronous conditions such as page faults, and device interrupts are asynchronous. CPU manuals use more specific categories.
- On Linux x86-64 the syscall number goes in `rax`, up to six arguments in registers, and the `syscall` instruction switches to ring 0; errors come back negative and glibc converts them to `-1` plus `errno`.
- Syscall overhead depends on the implementation and workload; batching, buffering and `io_uring` can amortise entry overhead.
- The vDSO runs read-only calls like `clock_gettime` in user mode, avoiding the syscall altogether.

questions.prompt: Classify each event: (1) a program executes `syscall` to call `read`; (2) a program touches a heap page for the first time and the kernel maps it; (3) a network card signals that a packet arrived. Which classification is right?

options.text: (1) trap, (2) interrupt, (3) exception
options.explanation: A page fault is synchronous: it is caused by the very instruction that ran. That makes it an exception, not an interrupt.

options.text: (1) trap, (2) exception, (3) interrupt
options.explanation: Correct. The syscall is a deliberate trap, the first-touch page fault is an exception caused by the current instruction, and the NIC signal is an asynchronous hardware interrupt.

options.text: (1) interrupt, (2) trap, (3) exception
options.explanation: This muddles deliberate versus external. A syscall isn't caused by external hardware, and a NIC packet isn't caused by the running instruction.

options.text: All three are interrupts
options.explanation: Some manuals use 'interrupt' loosely for everything, but the distinction matters: only (3) is asynchronous and unrelated to the running code.

questions.workedExample:
Ask two questions of each event:

1. **Is it caused by the instruction just executed?** If yes it's synchronous (trap or exception); if no it's an interrupt.
2. **Was it intended?** Intended means trap; an error or special condition means exception.

| Event | Caused by instr? | Intended? | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| `syscall` | yes | yes | trap |
| first touch | yes | no | exception |
| NIC packet | no | n/a | interrupt |

The page fault here isn't an error from the program's view: the kernel maps the page and re-runs the instruction.

questions.prompt: Why can't a malicious program enter kernel mode by jumping directly to the address of a privileged kernel function, such as the one that disables memory protection?

options.text: A jump doesn't change the CPU mode; only entry points registered by the kernel (syscall, exception and interrupt vectors) switch to kernel mode, and kernel pages aren't executable from user mode
options.explanation: Correct. Mode changes happen only through hardware-defined gates whose targets the kernel set at boot. A plain jump stays in user mode and faults on the kernel page.

options.text: The compiler refuses to generate such a jump
options.explanation: Attackers don't need a cooperating compiler; they can write machine code directly. Enforcement must be in hardware.

options.text: It can, which is why programs must run as root
options.explanation: Even root processes run in user mode. Root has more *permissions* checked by the kernel, not hardware privilege.

options.text: The kernel's addresses are secret, so the program can't find them
options.explanation: Address randomisation (KASLR) helps but isn't the main defence. Even with the address known, a user-mode jump into kernel memory faults.

questions.workedExample:
1. CPU mode is changed only by specific events: `syscall`/`sysenter`, exceptions and interrupts.
2. Each one jumps to an address the kernel configured (an MSR for `syscall`, the interrupt descriptor table for the rest).
3. A normal `jmp` keeps the current mode. Kernel pages are mapped as supervisor-only, so fetching an instruction from them in user mode causes a page fault.
4. So user code can choose *which* service (the number in `rax`), never *where* in the kernel to start.

Note the root point: root is a kernel permission check, not ring 0.

questions.prompt: A glibc C program calls `printf("x\n")` 1,000 times with stdout redirected to a regular file. Assume default full buffering with a buffer of at least 2,000 bytes, successful complete writes and normal exit. Roughly how many `write` syscalls carry that output?

options.text: Zero: `printf` writes directly to the file without the kernel
options.explanation: Writing to a file always needs the kernel. Buffering reduces syscalls; it can't remove the final one.

options.text: Exactly 1,000: one per `printf`
options.explanation: That would be the case for an unbuffered stream. When stdout is a file, glibc fully buffers it, so many calls share one `write`.

options.text: 2,000: one for the `x` and one for the newline
options.explanation: An unbuffered stream can cause much smaller writes, including single-character writes; there is no universal prohibition. The stated fully buffered setup combines output.

options.text: About 1: 2,000 bytes fit in the stdio buffer, which is flushed once at exit
options.explanation: Correct. When stdout isn't a terminal it's fully buffered (typically 4 KiB or more). 2,000 bytes fit, so the buffer is written once when the program exits.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each `printf` writes 2 bytes (`x` and `\n`) into glibc's stdout buffer.
2. Is stdout a terminal? No, it's a file, so it is **fully buffered**: newlines don't trigger a flush.
3. Total output is 1,000 × 2 = 2,000 bytes. The buffer is at least 4,096 bytes, so it never fills.
4. At `exit`, glibc flushes once: one `write(1, ..., 2000)`.

Run on a terminal instead and you'd see about 1,000 writes, because terminals are line-buffered. You can check both with `strace -e trace=write`.

questions.prompt: On Linux x86-64, a raw `syscall` returns `-9` in `rax` for a `write`. What does the program see if it called glibc's `write()` wrapper instead?

options.text: The program receives `SIGSEGV`
options.explanation: A bad file descriptor is an ordinary error return, not a fault.

options.text: `write` returns -9
options.explanation: The raw kernel convention returns a negated errno; glibc doesn't pass it through unchanged.

options.text: `write` returns -1 and `errno` is set to 9 (`EBADF`, bad file descriptor)
options.explanation: Correct. glibc sees a value in the range -4095 to -1, stores its negation in `errno`, and returns -1, the POSIX convention.

options.text: `write` returns 0 and `errno` is 9
options.explanation: 0 means zero bytes written, which isn't an error. glibc signals errors with -1.

questions.workedExample:
1. The kernel's ABI: success returns a non-negative result; failure returns `-errno`.
2. `-9` therefore means errno 9.
3. Errno 9 on Linux is `EBADF`: the fd isn't open (or not open for writing).
4. glibc's wrapper converts: `errno = 9; return -1;`.

So `perror("write")` would print `write: Bad file descriptor`. This is why you must check the return value *before* reading `errno`.

questions.prompt: You copy a 1 GiB file using `read`/`write` with a 4 KiB buffer, then with a 1 MiB buffer. Assume each syscall costs about 500 ns of overhead. Roughly how much syscall overhead does the larger buffer save?

options.text: About 0.5 ms
options.explanation: The 1 MiB case alone is about 1.024 ms for 2,048 calls, not 0.5 ms; the saving is about 261.12 ms.

options.text: About 261 ms
options.explanation: Correct. 4 KiB: 2 × 262,144 = 524,288 calls ≈ 262 ms. 1 MiB: 2 × 1,024 = 2,048 calls ≈ 1 ms. The saving is about 261 ms.

options.text: About 2.6 s
options.explanation: This is ten times too large. Recheck: 1 GiB / 4 KiB is 262,144 reads, not 2.6 million.

options.text: Nothing: the same bytes are copied either way
options.explanation: The bytes copied are the same, but the number of kernel entries isn't. Per-call overhead is paid per call, not per byte.

questions.workedExample:
Count syscalls (one `read` + one `write` per chunk):

```
4 KiB:  1 GiB / 4 KiB = 262,144
        x 2 calls     = 524,288
        x 500 ns      ~ 262 ms

1 MiB:  1 GiB / 1 MiB = 1,024
        x 2 calls     = 2,048
        x 500 ns      ~ 1 ms
```

Saving ≈ 261.12 ms under the supplied per-call assumption, ignoring an extra EOF check and short transfers. Copying and storage costs may dominate at larger sizes; a particular optimal buffer size requires measurement.

questions.prompt: Which can contribute to syscall overhead compared with a plain function call? Select all that apply.

options.text: Switching CPU mode and saving/restoring user registers
options.explanation: Correct. The `syscall`/`sysret` pair and the register save on the kernel stack are direct costs a function call doesn't have.

options.text: KPTI on Meltdown-affected CPUs switches page tables on entry and exit
options.explanation: Correct. Changing the page-table root costs time and (without PCID) flushes TLB entries.

options.text: Kernel code and data displace the program's cache lines and TLB entries
options.explanation: Correct. This *indirect* cost shows up as slower user code just after the syscall returns.

options.text: Every syscall forces a context switch to another process
options.explanation: Wrong. A syscall is a *mode switch* within the same process. A context switch only happens if the call blocks or the scheduler decides to preempt.

options.text: The kernel validates arguments and copies data across the boundary
options.explanation: Correct. The kernel can't trust user pointers, so it checks them and copies with `copy_from_user`/`copy_to_user`.

questions.workedExample:
Break the cost into parts:

1. **Mode switch + register save** (A): direct.
2. **Security mitigations** (B): KPTI page-table switch, Spectre barriers.
3. **Validation and copying** (E): the kernel treats user memory as hostile.
4. **Cache/TLB pollution** (C): the kernel's footprint evicts yours.

D is the common confusion. `getpid` does not inherently require another process to run. Blocking, preemption or other scheduling decisions can cause a context switch, including during a nonblocking syscall.

questions.prompt: `strace -c` on a busy logging service shows almost no `clock_gettime` syscalls, yet the code calls `clock_gettime` about 2 million times a second. What's the explanation?

options.text: The kernel batches the calls and handles them all at once
options.explanation: Syscalls aren't batched like this. Each would be a separate entry if it reached the kernel.

options.text: strace can't trace time-related syscalls
options.explanation: strace can trace any real syscall. The calls aren't showing because they never reach the kernel.

options.text: glibc caches the time and only refreshes it once a second
options.explanation: glibc doesn't cache the clock: that would return stale times. The fresh value comes from the vDSO.

options.text: The calls go through the vDSO, which reads kernel-maintained time data in user mode without entering the kernel
options.explanation: Correct. The vDSO page is mapped into each process; `clock_gettime` runs there, reading a shared data page and the CPU timestamp counter, so no syscall happens.

questions.workedExample: strace observes kernel entries, so calls completed by a supported vDSO fast path are absent. On x86-64 the vDSO exposes time-related functions and getcpu; exact support depends on the requested clock and clocksource. A fallback can occur for unsupported clock IDs or clocksources, so trace and inspect the actual environment rather than assuming a particular nanosecond cost.

questions.prompt: A program reads a framed TCP byte stream with `n = read(fd, buf, 65536);`. It returns 1,200. The code assumes it has the whole 65,536-byte frame. What is wrong?

options.text: 1,200 means an error code; check `errno`
options.explanation: Errors are signalled by -1. A positive return is the number of bytes actually read.

options.text: Nothing: `read` always waits for the full count on sockets
options.explanation: This is the misconception. On pipes and sockets, `read` returns as soon as *some* data is available.

options.text: `read` can return fewer bytes than requested (a short read); the code must loop until it has the full message
options.explanation: Correct. A short read is normal, not an error. Robust code loops, tracking how many bytes remain, or uses a framing protocol.

options.text: The kernel truncated the message, so the rest is lost
options.explanation: Nothing is lost. The remaining bytes arrive later and will be returned by subsequent reads.

questions.prompt: On x86-64 Linux, syscall arguments go in `rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9`, whereas the normal C function-calling convention uses `rcx` for the fourth argument instead of `r10`. Why?

options.text: `rcx` is reserved for the syscall number
options.explanation: The syscall number goes in `rax`.

options.text: The `syscall` instruction overwrites `rcx` with the user return address (and `r11` with RFLAGS), so the fourth argument can't live there
options.explanation: Correct. The hardware uses `rcx` to remember where to return to, so glibc's wrapper moves the fourth argument from `rcx` to `r10` before executing `syscall`.

options.text: `r10` is faster to read in kernel mode
options.explanation: Register access speed doesn't depend on privilege level or register number.

options.text: It's a historical bug that has never been fixed
options.explanation: It's a deliberate consequence of how the instruction is defined, not a bug.

questions.workedExample: On x86-64, SYSCALL stores the return instruction pointer in rcx and flags in r11, so Linux uses r10 for argument four. A named four-argument wrapper can move rcx to r10. The generic glibc syscall(number, ...) wrapper has an extra leading argument: it moves r8 to r10 while shifting the other arguments. SYSRET uses rcx/r11 on a suitable return path; Linux can also use IRET.
