questions.prompt: A server runs 10,000 threads, all busy doing short CPU work between requests, on 16 cores. Throughput is poor, but per-request CPU time looks fine in a profiler. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?

options.text: Too few threads; raise the count to 20,000
options.explanation: Each core already has about 625 runnable threads. Adding more increases preemption and cache thrashing.

options.text: About 625 runnable threads per core keep evicting each other's caches and TLB entries; use about one thread per core with non-blocking I/O
options.explanation: Oversubscription can add scheduler and cache costs. A smaller pool and nonblocking I/O are worth testing; counters and workload measurements must establish the actual bottleneck.

options.text: The kernel's run queue can't hold more than 1,024 threads
options.explanation: Linux has no such limit; run queues hold many thousands of tasks. The problem is cost, not capacity.

options.text: Each thread's 8 MiB stack uses up physical RAM
options.explanation: Stacks are reserved virtually and backed only by pages actually touched, so 10,000 threads don't use 80 GB of RAM.

questions.workedExample: 10,000 / 16 = 625 runnable threads per core under the simplified even-distribution assumption. This can cause scheduling contention and disrupt locality, but does not prove every cache is empty on every turn. Compare bounded worker pools, nonblocking I/O, CPU profiles and cache/scheduler counters. The appropriate worker count depends on blocking, CPU work and the service's shared data.

questions.prompt: Which statements about user-level (M:N) threads, such as Go goroutines, are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Switching between two goroutines on the same OS thread doesn't need to enter the kernel
options.explanation: The runtime can switch goroutines on an OS thread in user space, avoiding a kernel scheduling operation for that switch. No universal timing is implied.

options.text: A blocking syscall made by one user thread blocks the kernel thread underneath it
options.explanation: Correct. The kernel only sees the kernel thread. This is why M:N runtimes use non-blocking I/O and hand work to other kernel threads around blocking calls.

options.text: The kernel scheduler sees and schedules each goroutine individually
options.explanation: The kernel sees only the M kernel threads. Choosing which goroutine runs on them is the runtime's job.

options.text: M:N threads can run in parallel on several cores
options.explanation: Correct. That's the difference from N:1: the N user threads are spread over M kernel threads, which can run on different cores.

questions.workedExample:
Think about what the kernel can see:

- **Kernel view**: M kernel threads. It schedules those, possibly in parallel on several cores, so D is true.
- **Runtime view**: N goroutines multiplexed onto them. A switch between goroutines is a library call, so A is true, and the kernel never sees individual goroutines, so C is false.
- **Blocking**: if a goroutine traps into a blocking syscall, its kernel thread sleeps, so B is true. Go copes by handing the other goroutines to another thread.

lessons.title: Inter-process communication
lessons.summary: How isolated processes talk to each other on Linux, using pipes, signals, shared memory, message queues and sockets, and how to choose between them.
lessons.body:
Processes are isolated on purpose. Each has its own address space, so one can't read or scribble on another's memory. This can contain a tab-process fault, though shared resources, browser dependencies and privileged bugs can still affect other components.

But useful systems are made of processes that cooperate: a shell pipeline, a web server and its workers, a database and its client. **Inter-process communication (IPC)** is the set of kernel-provided channels that let isolated processes exchange data and events without giving up that isolation.

Think of processes as people in separate sealed offices. They can pass notes through a slot in the wall (pipes), ring a bell (signals), agree to share a whiteboard in a room between them (shared memory), use the internal post room (message queues), or pick up the phone (sockets). Each has a different cost, capacity and etiquette.

## Pipes: a one-way byte stream

A **pipe** is a kernel buffer with two file descriptors: one end to write, one end to read. `pipe(fd)` fills `fd[0]` with the read end and `fd[1]` with the write end (think "0 is stdin, 1 is stdout").

Pipes become useful with `fork`, because the child inherits both descriptors:

```c
int fd[2];
pipe(fd);
pid_t pid = fork();
if (pid == 0) {          /* child */
    close(fd[1]);
    char buf[64];
    ssize_t n;
    while ((n = read(fd[0], buf,
                     sizeof buf)) > 0)
        write(1, buf, n);
    _exit(0);
}
close(fd[0]);            /* parent */
const char *m = "hello\n";
write(fd[1], m, strlen(m));
close(fd[1]);   /* child now sees EOF */
waitpid(pid, NULL, 0);
```

The child prints `hello`. The rules that make this work:

- `read` on an empty pipe **blocks** until data arrives.
- `read` returns **0 (EOF)** only once *every* write end, in every process, is closed. That's why the child closes its inherited copy of `fd[1]`. If it didn't, it would wait forever for data from itself.
- `write` to a full pipe blocks until the reader drains it. Linux commonly defaults to 16 pages (64 KiB with 4 KiB pages), but resource limits and configuration can reduce it. Query `F_GETPIPE_SZ`; `F_SETPIPE_SZ` requests a resize subject to limits.
- `write` to a pipe with **no readers left** raises `SIGPIPE`, which kills the writer by default. If that signal is ignored, `write` fails with `EPIPE` instead.

### How the shell builds `ls | wc -l`

```
shell: pipe(fd)
  fork -> child 1:
          dup2(fd[1], 1)  stdout->pipe
          close both fds
          exec("ls")
  fork -> child 2:
          dup2(fd[0], 0)  stdin<-pipe
          close both fds
          exec("wc", "-l")
  close both fds; wait for both
```

Neither program knows a pipe is involved; they just use fds 0 and 1. When `ls` exits, the last write end closes, `wc` sees EOF and prints its count. This is the `fork`/`exec` gap from the previous lessons doing its job.

### Byte streams have no message boundaries

A pipe carries bytes, not messages. Two `write` calls of 10 bytes each may come out as one 20-byte `read`, or as 7 then 13. If you need messages, add framing: a length prefix, or a delimiter such as a newline.

### Atomic writes and `PIPE_BUF`

When several processes write to the same pipe, a write of at most **`PIPE_BUF`** bytes (4,096 on Linux; POSIX requires at least 512) is **atomic**: it won't be interleaved with other writers' data. Larger writes may be split and interleaved. This is why many processes can safely log short lines into one pipe.

### Named pipes (FIFOs)

Anonymous pipes commonly connect processes that inherit them, but descriptors can also be passed to unrelated processes over Unix sockets. A **FIFO** is a pipe with a name in the file system, so unrelated processes can find it:

```
$ mkfifo /tmp/jobs
$ cat /tmp/jobs &          # reader
$ echo "build" > /tmp/jobs # writer
build
```

The data still goes through a kernel buffer; nothing is written to disk.

## Signals: asynchronous notifications

A **signal** is a small integer delivered to a process to say "something happened". It carries almost no data, just the signal number (plus a little metadata with `SA_SIGINFO`). Signals are how the kernel and other processes interrupt you.

| Signal | Typical cause | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `SIGINT` (2) | Ctrl-C | terminate |
| `SIGTERM` (15) | `kill`, shutdown | terminate |
| `SIGKILL` (9) | `kill -9`, OOM killer | terminate |
| `SIGSEGV` (11) | bad memory access | core dump |
| `SIGPIPE` (13) | write to dead pipe | terminate |
| `SIGCHLD` (17) | child exited | ignore |

(Numbers are for Linux on x86 and ARM.) A process can, for most signals, **ignore** it, **block** it (hold it pending), or install a **handler**. `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP` are the exceptions: they can't be caught, blocked or ignored, though permissions, init semantics and uninterruptible waits can prevent or delay the expected effect.

The kernel delivers a pending signal when the target next returns from kernel to user mode: after a syscall, an interrupt or being scheduled. If a handler is installed, the kernel arranges for the process to run it, then resume where it was.

### Writing a safe handler

A handler can run *between any two instructions* of your program, including in the middle of `malloc` or `printf`. If the handler calls `malloc` too, the allocator's internal state may be half-updated and you get corruption or deadlock. Only **async-signal-safe** functions (listed in `signal-safety(7)`: `write`, `_exit`, `kill` and others) may be called. The standard pattern is to set a flag and do the real work in the main loop:

```c
static volatile sig_atomic_t stop;

static void on_term(int sig) {
    (void)sig;
    stop = 1;
}

int main(void) {
    struct sigaction sa = {0};
    sa.sa_handler = on_term;
    sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
    sigaction(SIGTERM, &sa, NULL);
    while (!stop)
        do_work();
    cleanup();   /* flush, close */
    return 0;
}
```

This is a schematic shutdown loop: include `<signal.h>`, define the work and cleanup routines, check sigaction errors and ensure do_work returns or responds to shutdown. A flag alone does not wake an indefinitely blocked operation. `docker stop` sends `SIGTERM`, waits a grace period (10 seconds by default), then sends `SIGKILL`. Kubernetes does the same with a 30-second default. A service that ignores `SIGTERM` gets killed mid-request.

> [!warning] Standard signals don't queue
> A standard signal is a single pending bit. If three children exit before your `SIGCHLD` handler runs, the handler may run once. Never count signals; reap in a `waitpid(-1, &st, WNOHANG)` loop while returns are positive; handle -1, including EINTR and ECHILD, as well as 0. Real-time signals (`SIGRTMIN` to `SIGRTMAX`) do queue.

Modern Linux code often avoids handlers altogether: `signalfd` turns signals into readable events on a file descriptor, which fits neatly into an `epoll` loop.

## Shared memory: avoiding payload copies

With pipes and sockets, data is copied twice: from the sender's buffer into the kernel, then from the kernel into the receiver's buffer, with a syscall on each side. **Shared memory** maps the *same physical pages* into both processes' address spaces. After setup, payload can be accessed with loads and stores without copying it through a kernel channel. Synchronisation, notification, cache coherence and page faults still have costs.

```c
/* creator initialises; peers attach */
int fd = shm_open("/stats",
                  O_CREAT | O_RDWR, 0600);
ftruncate(fd, 4096);
long *p = mmap(NULL, 4096,
               PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE,
               MAP_SHARED, fd, 0);
p[0] = 42; /* publish with proper sync */
```

On Linux, POSIX shared memory objects live in the `tmpfs` at `/dev/shm`. You can also share memory by `mmap`ing an ordinary file with `MAP_SHARED`, or by creating an anonymous `MAP_SHARED` mapping before `fork`.

The speed comes with responsibility:

- **No synchronisation is provided.** Two processes doing `p[0]++` can lose updates, exactly like two threads. Use a process-shared mutex or semaphore. Atomics require a platform/implementation that supports the chosen atomic representation across processes; non-lock-free atomics may use unsuitable process-local locks.
- **No notification.** The reader doesn't know new data has arrived. You need a semaphore, a futex, or a separate pipe or socket to say "look now".
- **Pointers don't travel.** The region may be mapped at different virtual addresses in each process, so store validated offsets or another relocatable representation rather than assuming raw pointers are usable.
- **Names outlive processes.** An object stays in `/dev/shm` until `shm_unlink` or reboot. A crashed process can leak it.

PostgreSQL is a classic user: each client connection is a separate backend process, and they all share the buffer cache and lock tables in shared memory. Chromium and many audio and video pipelines use shared memory to move large buffers between processes.

## Message queues: kernel-managed mailboxes

A **message queue** keeps message boundaries and lets unrelated processes exchange discrete messages through a named kernel object. POSIX queues (`mq_open`, `mq_send`, `mq_receive`) add a **priority** per message: `mq_receive` returns the oldest available message at the highest available priority.

```c
struct mq_attr a = {
    .mq_maxmsg = 10,
    .mq_msgsize = 256 };
mqd_t q = mq_open("/jobs",
                  O_CREAT | O_RDWR,
                  0600, &a);
mq_send(q, "resize img7", 12, 5);
```

Queues are bounded: on Linux the defaults allow 10 messages of up to 8 KiB, tunable under `/proc/sys/fs/mqueue/`. A full queue blocks `mq_send`, which gives natural back-pressure. The older System V API (`msgget`, `msgsnd`) still exists but is awkward; prefer POSIX. In practice many teams reach for sockets instead, because they work the same way locally and across a network.

## Sockets: bidirectional and general

**Unix domain sockets** (`AF_UNIX`) use the socket API but stay on one machine. They're addressed by a path such as `/var/run/docker.sock` or by an abstract name. Compared with pipes they are:

- **Bidirectional**: one connection carries requests and replies.
- **Client–server**: many clients can `connect` to one listening server, which `accept`s each.
- **Message-capable**: `SOCK_STREAM` is a byte stream, while `SOCK_DGRAM` and `SOCK_SEQPACKET` keep message boundaries (and on Unix sockets, datagrams are reliable).
- **Able to pass file descriptors**. With `sendmsg` and an `SCM_RIGHTS` control message, a process can hand an open fd to another. The receiver gets a new fd number referring to the same open file. Wayland clients pass buffer fds to the compositor this way, and privilege-separated servers use it so a privileged process opens files or sockets and gives them to a sandboxed worker.
- **Able to identify the peer**: `SO_PEERCRED` reports the connecting process's PID, UID and GID, checked by the kernel. PostgreSQL's `peer` authentication and the D-Bus daemon rely on this.

Because they skip the TCP/IP stack (no checksums, no congestion control, no loopback routing), Unix sockets avoid those TCP/IP protocol layers, but their performance relative to loopback TCP requires a workload-specific measurement. That's why PostgreSQL and MySQL clients use a Unix socket by default for local connections, and Redis can listen on one too.

**TCP sockets** provide the network-capable choice in this comparison; UDP and other network transports also exist. Writing to a socket interface means a service can later be split onto another host with little code change, which is a strong reason to default to sockets. D-Bus on Linux desktops and Android's Binder are higher-level IPC systems: D-Bus runs over Unix sockets, while Binder is its own kernel driver.

## Choosing a mechanism

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Stream between parent and child | pipe |
| Unrelated processes, simple stream | FIFO |
| "Stop", "reload", "child died" | signal |
| Bulk data, lowest latency | shared memory + a sync primitive |
| Discrete prioritised messages | POSIX message queue |
| Request/reply, fd passing, auth | Unix socket |
| Across machines | TCP socket |

A useful mental model is cost per message. Conventional read/write channel use often copies bytes into and out of kernel buffers. Batching and zero-copy APIs change the per-message costs, and a wake-up does not imply a fixed switch count. Shared memory avoids those payload copies but still pays synchronisation, coherence and notification costs. Large systems often combine them: a Unix socket for control messages and fd passing, and shared memory for the bulk data.

## Pitfalls

- **Forgetting to close unused pipe ends.** The reader never sees EOF because some process (often itself) still holds a write end. Close every end you don't use, straight after `fork`.
- **Assuming message boundaries on a stream.** One `write` doesn't equal one `read`. Frame your messages.
- **Unsafe signal handlers.** `printf`, `malloc` or taking a lock in a handler can deadlock. Set a flag or use `signalfd`.
- **Counting signals.** They coalesce. Reap children in a loop.
- **Dying on `SIGPIPE`.** A server writing to a client that disconnected is killed silently. Network servers usually ignore `SIGPIPE` and handle `EPIPE`, or pass `MSG_NOSIGNAL` to `send`.
- **Leaking named objects.** FIFOs, `/dev/shm` objects, message queues and socket paths persist after a crash. Unlink them on startup or shutdown.

> [!note] Content gap: IPC performance
> No reproducible IPC benchmark is supplied. Universal fastest-channel rankings and fixed copy/syscall counts are omitted. Code fragments illustrate mechanisms and need headers, error handling, ownership and synchronisation before production use.

## Key takeaways
- Pipes are one-way, bounded byte streams (query the actual Linux capacity); readers get EOF only when every write end is closed, and writes of up to `PIPE_BUF` (4,096) bytes are atomic.
- Signals are asynchronous notifications with almost no payload; `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP` can't be caught, standard signals don't queue, and handlers may only call async-signal-safe functions.
- Shared memory can avoid kernel-mediated payload copies, but requires synchronisation and notification; fastest depends on the workload.
- POSIX message queues keep message boundaries and priorities; Unix domain sockets are bidirectional, can pass file descriptors and verify peer credentials.
- Pick by need: pipes for simple streams, signals for events, shared memory for bulk data, sockets for request/reply and anything that might one day cross machines.

questions.prompt: After `int fd[2]; pipe(fd);`, which descriptor does the writer use?

options.explanation: `fd[0]` is the read end. It matches stdin being fd 0.
Correct. `fd[1]` is the write end, like stdout being fd 1. Data written there comes out of `fd[0]`.

options.text: Either; pipes are bidirectional
options.explanation: A pipe goes one way only. For two-way traffic you need two pipes or a socket pair.

options.text: Neither; you must call `open` on the pipe first
options.explanation: `pipe` returns two descriptors that are already open. Only a named FIFO needs `open`.

questions.workedExample:
Remember: **0 reads, 1 writes**, the same as stdin and stdout.

```
write(fd[1]) -> [buf] -> read(fd[0])
```

A shell sets up `a | b` by `dup2`ing `fd[1]` onto `a`'s stdout and `fd[0]` onto `b`'s stdin.

questions.prompt: A process has installed handlers for many signals. Which pair can still never be caught, blocked or ignored?

options.text: `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT`
options.explanation: Both can be caught. Graceful shutdown handlers depend on catching `SIGTERM`.

options.text: `SIGSEGV` and `SIGPIPE`
options.explanation: Both can be handled or (for `SIGPIPE`) ignored. Servers routinely ignore `SIGPIPE`.

options.text: `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP`
options.explanation: Applications cannot install handlers, block or ignore these signals. Permission checks, init exceptions and uninterruptible waits mean this is not a promise that every kill or stop request takes immediate effect.

options.text: `SIGCHLD` and `SIGHUP`
options.explanation: Both can be caught. Daemons often treat `SIGHUP` as "reload config".

questions.workedExample: SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, blocked or ignored by normal application signal handling. They provide forced termination or stopping without application cleanup, but a caller still needs permission and kernel/init/wait rules affect delivery and timing.

questions.prompt: Two processes exchange large video frames many times a second. Which mechanism avoids copying each frame through the kernel?

options.text: A pipe
options.explanation: Each frame would be copied from the writer into the kernel buffer, then out again to the reader.

options.text: A Unix domain socket
options.explanation: Sockets copy data through kernel buffers just as pipes do, though they can pass an fd to a shared buffer.

options.text: Shared memory
options.explanation: Correct. Both processes map the same physical pages. Writing a frame is ordinary stores, and the reader sees it without any copy.

options.text: Signals
options.explanation: Signals carry a number, not data. They can say "frame ready" but can't carry the frame.

questions.workedExample: Conventional pipe/socket read-write transfers normally copy payload through kernel buffers. Shared mappings let sender and receiver access the same storage, with an explicit ownership/publication protocol. Synchronisation or notification may make syscalls, and page faults or zero-copy alternatives change costs; the benefit here is avoiding the normal intermediate payload copies.

questions.prompt: A process does two writes to a pipe: `write(fd, "HELLO", 5)` then `write(fd, "WORLD", 5)`. The reader calls `read(fd, buf, 100)` once, after both writes. What can it get?

options.text: Always exactly `HELLO`, because each write is one message
options.explanation: Pipes are byte streams with no message boundaries. Nothing records where one write ended.

options.text: `HELLOWORLD` in one read
options.explanation: Correct. Both writes are in the buffer, and `read` returns whatever is available, up to 100 bytes.

options.text: An error, because the reader asked for more than was written
options.explanation: `read` returning fewer bytes than requested is normal, not an error.

options.text: `WORLD`, because the buffer is last in, first out
options.explanation: Pipes are first in, first out. Bytes come out in the order they were written.

questions.workedExample:
1. After both writes the kernel buffer holds the 10 bytes `HELLOWORLD`.
2. `read(fd, buf, 100)` returns whatever is available, up to 100: here 10 bytes.
3. The boundary between the two writes is gone.

If message boundaries matter, frame the data (a length prefix, or newline-terminated lines), or use something that keeps boundaries, such as a message queue or a `SOCK_SEQPACKET` socket.

options.text: The parent should have closed `fd[0]` later
options.explanation: The parent closing its read end is correct. The hang is on the child's side.

options.text: The child never closed its own copy of `fd[1]`, so a write end is still open and `read` never returns 0
options.explanation: Correct. EOF needs *every* write end closed. The child inherited one and still holds it, so it waits for data from itself.

options.text: The buffer of 64 bytes is too small
options.explanation: A small buffer only means more loop iterations. It can't cause a hang.

options.text: `waitpid` blocks the pipe
options.explanation: `waitpid` waits for the child to exit and has no effect on the pipe.

questions.workedExample:
Count the open write ends after `fork`:

```
parent fd[1]: open -> closed later
child  fd[1]: open (never closed!)
```

1. The child reads the three lines.
2. The buffer is empty, but one write end (its own) is still open, so `read` blocks instead of returning 0.
3. The parent waits for the child, and the child waits for EOF: a hang.

Fix: `close(fd[1]);` as the child's first line.

questions.prompt: In bash, `yes | head -n 1` prints `y` and finishes at once, and `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` is 141. What happened to `yes`?

options.text: It exited normally with status 141
options.explanation: Bash status alone is ambiguous because a program can explicitly return 141. In this standard yes/head pipeline with default signal handling, the broken pipe explains SIGPIPE termination.

options.text: `head` sent it `SIGTERM`
options.explanation: `head` doesn't signal anyone. It just exits, closing the read end.

options.text: It was killed by `SIGPIPE` after writing to a pipe with no readers
options.explanation: Correct. 141 − 128 = 13, which is `SIGPIPE`. Once `head` exited, `yes`'s next write had nowhere to go.

options.text: The pipe filled up and `yes` was killed by the OOM killer
options.explanation: A full pipe just blocks the writer; it uses no extra memory. The OOM killer sends `SIGKILL` (137).

questions.workedExample:
1. `head -n 1` reads a line, prints `y` and exits, closing the only read end.
2. `yes` keeps writing. A write to a pipe with no readers raises `SIGPIPE`.
3. The default action is to terminate, so `yes` dies.
4. Shells report a signal death as 128 + N: 128 + 13 = 141.

This is the behaviour you want for pipelines: producers stop automatically when the consumer has finished.

questions.prompt: A blocking Linux pipe is confirmed with F_GETPIPE_SZ to have 65,536-byte capacity and starts empty. A reader keeps its end open but never reads. A writer repeatedly writes 4,096 bytes successfully. How many writes fill it before the next blocks?

options.explanation: One write occupies only 4,096 bytes of the explicitly supplied 65,536-byte capacity.
Correct. 65,536 / 4,096 = 16 writes fill the buffer, so the 17th blocks.
That would mean 1 KiB per write. Each write here is 4 KiB.

options.text: None ever block; the kernel grows the buffer
options.explanation: The pipe is bounded. A full pipe blocks the writer, which is how back-pressure works.

questions.workedExample:
```
capacity = 64 KiB = 65,536 bytes
write    = 4,096 bytes
65,536 / 4,096 = 16 writes
```

The 17th `write` blocks until the reader drains some space (or fails with `EAGAIN` if the fd is non-blocking). A bounded buffer is what makes a fast producer slow down to a slow consumer's speed. `fcntl(fd, F_SETPIPE_SZ, n)` can resize it, up to `/proc/sys/fs/pipe-max-size`.

questions.prompt: Which of these is it safe to do inside a signal handler? Select all that apply.

options.text: Call `write(2, "bye\n", 4)`
options.explanation: Correct. `write` is on the async-signal-safe list, because it's a plain syscall with no hidden user-space state.

options.text: Call `printf("got %d\n", sig)`
options.explanation: Not safe. `printf` uses stdio buffers and locks. If the handler interrupted another `printf`, they can be corrupted or deadlock.

options.text: Set a `volatile sig_atomic_t` flag
options.explanation: Correct. That's the standard pattern: the handler sets a flag and the main loop acts on it.

options.text: Call `malloc` to build a message
options.explanation: Not safe. If the signal arrived during `malloc`, the allocator's state is half-updated or its lock is held.

options.text: Call `_exit(1)`
options.explanation: Correct. `_exit` is async-signal-safe. (Plain `exit` isn't, because it runs `atexit` handlers and flushes stdio.)

questions.workedExample: Use the documented async-signal-safe list; being a library wrapper or syscall alone is not the criterion. write and _exit are listed, while printf and malloc are not. A volatile sig_atomic_t flag supports communication with the interrupted execution, but is not general thread synchronisation. Preserve errno if the handler changes it. signalfd is an alternative when the selected signals are blocked in the appropriate threads.

questions.prompt: A parent forks 3 children. Its `SIGCHLD` handler does `reaped++; waitpid(-1, NULL, WNOHANG);`. All three children exit within microseconds of each other. What can `reaped` be once things settle?

options.text: Always 3
options.explanation: This assumes one handler call per child. Standard signals don't queue, so several exits can merge into one delivery.

options.text: Anywhere from 1 to 3, and some children may stay zombies
options.explanation: Correct. Pending `SIGCHLD`s coalesce into one bit. Each handler run reaps only one child, so unreaped children stay zombies.

options.text: Always 1
options.explanation: Coalescing can happen, but it isn't guaranteed. If the exits are spread out enough, the handler can run two or three times.

options.text: 0, because `SIGCHLD` is ignored by default
options.explanation: Ignored by default, yes, but this process installed a handler, so the handler runs.

questions.workedExample:
1. Child 1 exits: `SIGCHLD` becomes pending.
2. Children 2 and 3 exit before the handler runs: it's *already* pending, so nothing is added.
3. The handler runs once: `reaped = 1`, one child is reaped, and two are left as zombies.

With different timing you get 2 or 3. The fix is to loop:

```c
while (waitpid(-1, NULL,
       WNOHANG) > 0)
    reaped++;
```

questions.prompt: Twenty worker processes share one pipe to a logging process. Workers A and B write records with a single `write` each. A's records are 200 bytes; B's are 10 KiB. What can the logger see?

options.text: Neither A's nor B's records are ever interleaved
options.explanation: Only writes of up to `PIPE_BUF` (4,096 bytes on Linux) are guaranteed atomic. 10 KiB is over the limit.

options.text: A's writes are not interleaved with other writers' bytes, though reads can split them; B's writes may be interleaved
options.explanation: Correct. 200 ≤ 4,096, so each of A's writes lands in one piece. B's 10 KiB writes can be split and mixed with other data.

options.text: Both may be interleaved, because pipes give no atomicity at all
options.explanation: POSIX guarantees atomicity for writes of up to `PIPE_BUF` bytes. That guarantee is what makes shared log pipes work.

options.text: B's records are rejected with `EINVAL`
options.explanation: Large writes are allowed. They just lose the atomicity guarantee.

questions.workedExample:
1. `PIPE_BUF` on Linux is 4,096 bytes.
2. A: 200 ≤ 4,096, so each write is atomic and is never interleaved.
3. B: 10,240 > 4,096, so the kernel may copy it in pieces as space frees up, and other writers' data can land in between.

Fixes for B: keep records under 4 KiB, give each worker its own pipe, or use a `SOCK_DGRAM` or `SOCK_SEQPACKET` Unix socket, which delivers each message whole.

questions.prompt: A privileged daemon accepts TCP connections and wants to hand each connected socket to a long-running sandboxed worker process. What should it use?

options.text: Write the fd number into shared memory
options.explanation: File descriptor numbers are indexes into each process's own fd table. Number 7 in the daemon means nothing in the worker.

options.text: Send the fd over a Unix domain socket with `sendmsg` and `SCM_RIGHTS`
options.explanation: Correct. The kernel installs a new descriptor in the receiver that refers to the same open socket.

options.text: Send the fd through a pipe with `write`
options.explanation: That would only send the integer, which, as with shared memory, means nothing in another process.

options.text: Signal the worker with `SIGUSR1` so it opens the connection itself
options.explanation: A signal carries no data, and the worker can't take over a TCP connection that's already been accepted.

questions.workedExample:
1. An fd is a per-process index into a table of open files. Copying the integer doesn't copy the access.
2. Only the kernel can add an entry to another process's fd table.
3. Unix domain sockets offer exactly that: attach the fd to a message as `SCM_RIGHTS` ancillary data.
4. The worker's `recvmsg` returns a new fd (perhaps a different number) for the same connection.

The other ways to share an fd are inheriting it across `fork`, or `pidfd_getfd` on newer kernels, but neither suits an already-running, unrelated worker as cleanly.

questions.prompt: Two processes share a counter in a POSIX shared memory region from `shm_open` + `mmap(MAP_SHARED)`. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: If both do `p[0]++` with no synchronisation, updates can be lost
options.explanation: Correct. `++` is a load, an add and a store. Two processes can both load 5 and both store 6, just as two threads can.

options.text: The kernel serialises writes to shared pages, so no locking is needed
options.explanation: The kernel isn't involved in loads and stores to mapped memory at all. That's why it's fast, and why it can't help here.

options.text: If a process crashes without calling `shm_unlink`, the object stays in `/dev/shm`
options.explanation: Correct. The name persists until unlinked or reboot, which can leak memory.

options.text: A pointer stored in the region may be invalid in the other process
options.explanation: Correct. The region can be mapped at different virtual addresses, so store offsets from the base instead.

options.text: For large transfers it is slower than a pipe because of page faults
options.explanation: Shared memory can avoid payload copies, but later page faults, cache coherence and synchronisation still matter. The claim that it is necessarily slower is unsupported.

questions.workedExample: Unsynchronised increments can lose updates. Use a process-shared mutex/semaphore, or atomics whose implementation supports cross-process use. A named shared-memory object persists until unlinked (or its backing environment is removed); mappings may have different virtual addresses, so use validated offsets. Shared memory can avoid kernel payload copies, but it does not guarantee zero later faults or universally better performance.
